summary: This paper establishes a theoretical framework for implementing Josephson-like qubits using easy-plane magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) by exploiting the mathematical isomorphism between low-dissipation MTJ spin dynamics and superconducting Josephson junction physics. The authors develop a Hamiltonian formalism identifying three distinct MTJ-based qubit types—transmon, flux, and charge—and derive conditions on anisotropy constants, Gilbert damping $\alpha \lesssim 10^{-3}$, resonance frequency $\omega_r \sim 10^{10}$ rad/s, and temperature $T \lesssim 0.36$ K for quantum operation.
motivation: MTJs are CMOS-compatible and industrially deployed in memory applications, making them attractive alternatives to Josephson junctions for scalable quantum integration without requiring millikelvin operation, despite Josephson junctions' proven success in quantum computing.
method: The authors derive an effective Lagrangian and Hamiltonian from the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation under low-dissipation conditions ($\omega_d \ll \omega_r$), establishing correspondence with Josephson junction theory where azimuthal angle $\varphi$ and magnetization projection $M_z$ play roles analogous to phase and charge operators, then systematically analyze different energy scale hierarchies to realize transmon, flux, and charge qubit analogs.
result: Transmon and flux MTJ qubits are feasible with realistic parameters: $\hbar\omega_{01} \sim 10^{-17}$ to $10^{-16}$ erg, $T_1 \sim 1$ µs coherence times comparable to Josephson qubits, tunable effective damping via spin current injection to suppress decoherence, and critical temperatures up to $\sim 360$ mK for ferromagnets (relaxable to 1 K using ferrimagnets/antiferromagnets with $\omega_r \sim 1$ THz).
